title: Read and validate query parameters
description:
Implement Search, a handler for a search endpoint that reads two parameters out of the query part of the request.

A request that is accepted replies 200 with a body naming both parameters, exactly in this shape and with no trailing newline: Search(target: "/search?q=go&page=3") -> "q=go page=3".

The rules for the two parameters:

- q is required. Its value is whatever the client sent, already unescaped for you: "/search?q=go+lang&page=2" -> "q=go lang page=2", and "/search?q=caf%C3%A9&page=1" -> "q=café page=1".
- page is optional and defaults to 1 when the client did not send it at all: "/search?q=go" -> "q=go page=1".
- Parameters you were not asked about are none of your business: "/search?q=go&page=10&sort=new" -> "q=go page=10".

Everything else is rejected with 400. The body of a rejection is not checked, only the status. A request is rejected when:

- q is missing, or was sent with an empty value. Sending it empty is not the same as not sending it, and both are refused here — but they are refused for different reasons, and only one of them is the absence you have to detect for page.
- page was sent with an empty value. This one is a rejection, not the default: the client asked for a page and named none.
- page is not a whole number, or is below 1.
- q or page was sent more than once. A parameter carries a list of values, not one value; reading only the first would let "/search?q=go&page=1&page=2" through as page 1.
- The query part as a whole is not well formed, even when the parameters you need are readable from it: "/search?q=go&junk=%zz" -> 400, and "/search?q=go&a=1;b=2" -> 400. Both of these are malformed, and the convenient way of reading parameters answers them by quietly discarding whatever it could not understand and reporting no problem at all, so a handler built on it replies 200 to both. Reach for the parsing call that hands you the error instead of swallowing it, and give it the unparsed query text off the request.
objective: Practice reading parameters out of a request's query, telling an absent parameter apart from an empty one and from a repeated one, and refusing a malformed query instead of letting the convenient accessor discard it in silence.

title: Rebuild the absolute URL of a request
description:
Implement CanonicalURL. It receives a server's incoming request and returns the absolute URL the client asked for, as text, rebuilt from the request: CanonicalURL(request for "/files/a/b?x=1" addressed to ex.com) -> "http://ex.com/files/a/b?x=1".

Four pieces go into it, and each one has a catch.

- The scheme is https when the request arrived over a secure connection and http when it did not. There is a field on the request that is set only in the secure case; the URL held on a server request never carries a scheme of its own, so it cannot tell you this.
- The authority is the host the client addressed, port included when there was one: a request addressed to virtual.example:8443 -> "http://virtual.example:8443/a". The URL held on a server request has an empty authority — for an incoming request it is carried separately, on the request itself.
- The path must go back out exactly as it came in on the wire, with the client's percent-escapes preserved: request for "/files/a%2Fb?x=1" -> "http://ex.com/files/a%2Fb?x=1". The field that is easiest to reach for holds the *decoded* path, where that escaped slash has become an ordinary one, and using it here silently rewrites the request into a different one. There is an accessor that gives you back the form that can go on the wire; it is always right, unlike the raw field behind it, which is left empty whenever the escaping was unremarkable — "/x%20y" -> "http://ex.com/x%20y" is one such case.
- The query is appended after a question mark, exactly as sent and not re-encoded: "/caf%C3%A9?q=a%2Fb" -> "http://ex.com/caf%C3%A9?q=a%2Fb". When there was no query, the question mark is left off entirely: request for "/items" -> "http://ex.com/items", and a request for "/items?" with nothing after the mark is treated the same way.

A request for "/" returns "http://ex.com/".
objective: Practice reassembling the URL a client asked for from an incoming request: the scheme from the connection, the authority from the request rather than the URL, and the path in the escaped form that survives a round trip instead of the decoded one.

title: Read a header and a cookie, issue and clear one
description:
Implement Session, a handler that reads the caller's session cookie and issues one when there is none.

A session is identified by a cookie named sid. What the handler does depends on how many of those the request carries:

- None: start one. The value for the new session comes from a request header named X-Session-Token, or is the word anon when that header was not sent. Reply 200 with the body "new " followed by that value — Session(no cookies, no header) -> "new anon", and Session(no cookies, header X-Session-Token: t-42) -> "new t-42" — and send the new cookie back to the client with the value you just used.
- Exactly one: resume it. Reply 200 with the body "resume " followed by that cookie's value, and send no cookie back. Cookies with other names are irrelevant to this count: a request carrying theme=dark and sid=abc and lang=pt -> "resume abc", while one carrying only theme=dark and lang=pt is the none case above.
- More than one: refuse. Two cookies named sid, which is what a client that was issued one at two different scopes will send, is an ambiguous session rather than a resumable one. Reply 409 and send no cookie back. The obvious way of reading a cookie by name hands you the first one and no hint that a second exists; there is a separate accessor, newer than it, that returns every cookie carrying the name.

Bodies are compared exactly and none ends in a newline.

The cookie you issue for a new session must carry four protections and a scope, none of which are defaults — a cookie built from a name and a value alone has all of them switched off:

- it is scoped to the whole site, so it comes back on every path rather than only the one that set it
- it lives for one hour
- it is not reachable from scripts running in the page
- it never travels over a plain connection
- it is withheld from cross-site subrequests, while still being sent on ordinary top-level navigation from another site — the middle of the three settings for this, not the strictest one

Finally, a request made with the DELETE method ends the session, whether or not one was running: reply 200 with the body "bye", and send back a cookie that clears sid — same name, an empty value, expiring immediately, and carrying the same scope as the one you issued, since a clearing cookie that does not match the original's scope replaces nothing and the old cookie keeps arriving.
objective: Practice the cookie round trip: counting the cookies that share a name rather than taking the first, falling back to a header when none is present, and issuing one with its scope, lifetime and protections spelled out — then clearing it with a matching scope.
